description: 60 years on from the opening of the BT Tower, and amidst its sale to a hotel consortium, participants are invited on a research-led walk around Fitzrovia to reflect on the hidden stories and unseen infrastructures that contribute to the creation of the city and its green spaces.

factsheet.heading: Context
paragraphs: When the BT Tower opened in 1965, it was heralded as a symbol of ‘the technical and architectural skills of this modern age’. Offering the possibility of instantaneous telephonic and televisual communication, it was an icon of publicly owned national infrastructure.

For decades, the tower relied on clear, uninterrupted microwave paths routed through a network of repeater stations in outer London and the home counties. Any tall building constructed within these corridors risked causing signal loss or distortion. The BT Tower therefore acted as a brake on development in this part of the West End, shaping both the skyline and the formation of public squares and parks.

Sixty years on, in the context of the tower’s planned re-development into a hotel and leisure facility, this guided walk invites you to think about ‘signals and sightlines’ in new ways, reflecting on what we can’t see as well as what we can - tracing and recording a series of sightlines to the tower from parks, squares, and incidental green spaces in Fitzrovia.

factsheet.heading: Guides
paragraphs: Led by artist-researcher and London National Park City Ranger Jordan Rowe, and cultural historian Dr David Anderson, the walk will culminate at the London National Park City Visitors Centre on Mortimer Street for refreshments. An evening launch event for the project's audio guide and publication will follow (please book for this element via the 'London National Park City Visitors Centre' listing).

factsheet.heading: Support
paragraphs: With thanks to the London National Park City Foundation, the UCL Department of Geography, and The Building Centre.
